chapter_theme: After the lovers' quarrel in which Ilakkanai mistakes Civakan's tears for thoughts of other women, the parrot's mock death ends it and the wedding days pass; Civakan then rides the elephant Culamani in state through the city.

cast.role: the hero, now a king, wedding Ilakkanai; called Sunandai's son in 2521
Govindan's daughter, Civakan's new bride; unnamed in these verses
the household parrot that threatens to hang itself to end the quarrel
the myna and parrot of the household, who plead for Civakan
the women of Ilakkanai's household, who scold the birds
the kings and armies who accompany Civakan in procession

2503.reading: The bridegroom, whose body smells of ghee and whose chest is a flower, sinks into a sea of desire as the bed of flowers delights.
2503.nuance: The first half-lines (a smoke-scented, ghee-touched young body) are hard to join, so the sense of the opening is taken from the closing line, where the man sinks in the sea of desire.
2503.event: Civakan and his bride, on a flower couch, give themselves to love.

2504.reading: The bride, clinging to the garlanded chest as lightning clings to the cloud that swallows it, is spent and lies like a vine that has dropped away.
2504.nuance: Line 2 is obscure and the simile is read from lines 3 and 4 only.
2504.event: The bride lies clasped to Civakan's chest and then goes slack.

2505.reading: The garlanded man and the girl, not knowing it is wrong, delight in each other and lie on a silk bed on which incense smokes, drunk on the wine of love.
2505.nuance: The words in line 2 (எய் உணர் வாமி தென்று அறியாது) could mean they do not know how the night passes or that they do not heed what is forbidden; the reading takes the first.
2505.event: The pair lie together on the silk bed, drunk with desire.

2506.reading: Civakan gazes at her beauty without blinking until his eyes smart and water; she takes the tears for tears shed thinking of other women, says 'let this folly join those who weep for others', and her spear eyes spit fire in anguish.
2506.nuance: Her accusation rests on a misreading: the tears come from not blinking at her, so the sulk is a lovers' quarrel the verse itself shows to be groundless.
2506.event: Civakan's tears of rapt gazing make Ilakkanai suspect he is thinking of other women, and she flares in a sulk.

2507.reading: Angry, she wipes off the sandal, snaps her garland, scatters her jewels, wrings the gold ring on her gem-like finger, sobs, lets her brows crinkle and stands with her lotus face sweating.
2507.event: Ilakkanai tears off her ornaments in her sulk and stands sobbing.

2508.reading: The prince lies clasping her tender feet while her eyes, red as lamps, shed tears like black pearls, and she, her life as if broken, weeps with him.
2508.nuance: The simile of tears like black pearls rests on a doubtful word in line 3 (பொழிப் வே).
2508.event: Civakan falls at Ilakkanai's feet while she weeps.

2509.reading: Seeing the bough that bore the sprout weep from burning eyes, he asks whom he can tell the fruit of his old sin, and bids the bees stroke her and ask her to give him the boon.
2509.nuance: The karma claim is a lover's figure of speech for an undeserved quarrel, not a teaching; and it is the husband, not the narrator, who blames an old deed for a wrong he has not done.
2509.event: Civakan, unable to hide her tears, begs the bees to plead with her for forgiveness.

claims.claim: present suffering is the fruit of sin done in an earlier life

2510.reading: The myna and the parrot, hearing, look through the cage-holes and say among themselves: is the king's daughter's heart stone or does it relent; we melt and the prince is faultless; let us beg our gracious lady.
2510.nuance: In line 3 the words சாவம் யாம் உருகி are doubtful; the sense of pleading for the faultless man is taken from the whole verse.
2510.event: The household parrot and myna, watching the quarrel, decide to plead for Civakan.

2511.reading: The women, 'myna-like' with their reasoned words, scold the birds: you eat the food she gives every day and still dare to speak; if you say more she will show you no food for three days, so shut your mouths.
2511.nuance: The speaker is taken to be the household women (பூவையார்); the word may instead denote the myna, so the speaker is not certain. The birds are addressed as தத்தை (parrot).
2511.event: The women of the house silence the parrot and myna with the threat of withheld food.

2512.reading: A speech that, though stained with blame, he who has worshipped her small feet asks that she become the goddess he serves and grant the boon, and that she cease to be like a tied elephant that melts and does not look back.
2512.nuance: Line 4 (பிழிசடு கோதை போலாம் பெண்டிரைக் கெடப் பிறந்தாள்) does not parse and the speaker is inferred from the plea; the sense is not settled.
2512.event: Civakan pleads with Ilakkanai in the language of worship.

2513.reading: The parrot cries that even were it the bride's own mother it would not live to see this, and it will die, and ties itself with a thread; she, bewildered, laughs; he cries 'live long, I have won the boon', embraces her and praises her ornaments.
2513.nuance: The sulk ends only when a third party, the pet, stages a death; neither of the lovers yields first.
2513.event: The parrot's mock hanging breaks Ilakkanai's sulk and Civakan embraces her.

2514.reading: Addressing the blue lily, he says it does not match her long dark eyes even if it stays in the flood in long penance, and asks whether its laughing colour is that, or the street of the wine-drinkers; long may the lily live.
2514.nuance: The refrain வாழி நீலம் can be taken as a blessing to the lily or as a name; the verse is read as his praise of her eyes against the flower.

2515.reading: The shy girl, laughing that the parrot and myna have blamed the faultless, gives the golden-chested lord the nectar of her smiling face, and no lute-song is needed to lay the quarrel to rest.
2515.nuance: Line 1 (பாண் குலாய்ப் படுக்கல் வேண்டா) is obscure and is read as 'no song need be sung to soothe her'.
2515.event: Ilakkanai laughs at the birds' scene and ends the sulk with a smile for Civakan.

2516.reading: Like a king who enters the hostile land and shakes it, the man shakes her beauty away; the peacock-like plume droops, her anklets weep and the honey-garland snaps so that honey runs.
2516.nuance: The conquering-king simile in line 2 and 3 casts lovemaking as invasion of a foe; it is the poet's, and it sits oddly beside the sulk just ended.
2516.event: Civakan and Ilakkanai make love, her garland and anklets breaking.

2517.reading: Her eyes like spear, sword and blue lily, she clings to his broad chest as the kalpaka tree entwines the creeper of love that has flowered and grown lovely.
2517.event: Ilakkanai clings to Civakan's chest after the reconciliation.

2518.reading: The peacock-like woman and the lion-like king, bound by love and twined together, let the seven appointed days go by.
2518.nuance: Line 2 (மணிக்கந் தன்னதோள்) is garbled in the edition; the seven days are clear from line 4.
2518.event: The couple spend the seven days of the wedding together.

2519.reading: They are anointed with sandal and powder and adorned with garland, gold thread and earrings, the pearl strings set about them.
2519.nuance: The edition prints strange forms here (மோட்டி, மோட்டு) and the subject of the plural verb is taken to be the two.
2519.event: The pair dress for the wedding ceremony after the seven days.

2520.reading: He wears green silk, the garland on his chest and the line of ornaments, and to the deer-eyed women with their wondering look he becomes one who consumes their flesh and life together.
2520.nuance: The last line (ஊனு யிருணு மொருவ னாயினான்) is corrupt; the sense given is only a guess.
2520.event: Civakan dresses and is seen by the women.

2521.reading: Sunandai's son, the bees drinking from the rutting streams of an elephant of three musths, mounts it while the bowed yak-tail fans and the conches sound.
2521.nuance: Civakan is named as Sunandai's son, the foster mother who raised him, in the very verse in which he rides as a king.
2521.event: Civakan mounts a state elephant with fans and conches.

2522.reading: On the elephant called Culamani, among a hundred cow elephants, laden with sugarcane and paddy, the garlanded king mounts treading on the crowns of kings.
2522.nuance: The phrase மன்னர் முடிமிதித்தேறினான் may mean the kings bow so that he mounts over their crowns, or that he rides over them; it is read as a figure for their submission.
2522.event: Civakan rides the elephant Culamani, the other kings' crowns beneath him.

2523.reading: His umbrella of gold, silver, diamond and pearl hung with coral stems makes him look like the sun in its shade.

2524.reading: The kings crowd round with whisks while he rides an elephant like the moon pouring beams, with drums and shouts, and the king enters the street with his sea of troops.
2524.event: Civakan, with the kings about him, enters the street in procession.

2525.reading: Horses spread like rain, golden chariots fill the ground and elephants and warriors crowd without a gap.
2525.nuance: Line 1-2, with the horse's hooves shamed by the ground and the hair flying like wings, is a stock simile and its grammar is loose.

2526.reading: The city of banners is loud like the sea that takes the rain as the women who have killed the palmyra's shoots with their breasts go to see her husband.
2526.nuance: The subject in lines 1 and 2 is difficult and the identity of the woman who is said to go to see her husband is not settled.
2526.event: The people go to see the bridegroom as the city roars.

links.note: Kural 1320 has the sulking woman accuse a man who only sits gazing at her of thinking of someone else; here Civakan's unblinking gaze and watering eyes make Ilakkanai say he weeps thinking of others.
links.teaches: The epic shows that the suspicion in the couplet can grow from the very rapture of the gaze, so the quarrel is a love's misreading and not a sign of a wandering heart.

gains.a: the sulk is placed in the Kural's recognised pattern of a wife who suspects her husband for what he does with his eyes
gains.b: a story in which the suspicion is false and ends in laughter, which the couplet does not tell

links.note: Kural 1329 has the man wish the sulk would go on and the night lengthen so he might keep pleading; Civakan, pleading through the bees, calls her anger the fruit of his own past sin.
links.teaches: Where the couplet relishes the plea as part of love's game, the epic lets the husband feel the quarrel as an undeserved punishment, so the same scene reads as pleasure or as pain by the speaker's mood.

gains.a: his plea is shown to be, in the Kural's terms, a stage of love's play that he has not yet found pleasing
gains.b: the cost of the pleading, which the couplet leaves out, the fear that one's love is being punished for a past wrong

links.note: Kural 1327 says the one who yields in a lovers' quarrel wins; Civakan yields first, but the quarrel ends when the parrot threatens to hang itself.
links.teaches: Yielding does not by itself end the sulk in the epic; it takes the comic shock from a third party to break it, which limits the couplet's rule that the loser wins.

gains.a: Civakan's earlier abasement is shown to be only half of what wins her, as the Kural's rule would suggest
gains.b: a case where a rule about the two lovers alone needs an outside agent, here the pet

links.note: Naladiyar 384 praises a wife who knows when to sulk and relents sweetly; Ilakkanai relents only when the birds' scene makes her laugh, and gives the smile as her reward.
links.teaches: The quatrain's wife relents of her own judgment, while the epic's wife is brought round by a joke at her own expense, so the ideal is softened by what the story shows of how quarrels actually end.

gains.a: Ilakkanai's smile is read as the sweet relenting the quatrain prizes in a wife
gains.b: the quatrain's ideal is given a scene that shows what makes a sulk melt

links.note: Gunamalai's red-beaked parrot, her only refuge, was made her go-between in love; here the household parrot, with its mock death, becomes the go-between that ends a lovers' quarrel.
links.teaches: The parrot appears again as the love-story's helper, but at Gunamalai's side it carries a plea across a distance while at Ilakkanai's it mends a quarrel within the bed-chamber.

links.note: 2326 had the victor bathed as for anointing with the blood of crowned kings, joined to the Earth goddess; now, riding Culamani, he treads on the crowns of kings.
links.teaches: The anointing promised in the battle's aftermath is fulfilled in the procession, where the defeated and allied kings' crowns are laid beneath the hero as a public sign of his rule.

links.note: After the victory, 2327 had him enter the old city worshipped by its people; now, wedded, he rides into the street among kings with whisks and drums.
links.teaches: The victor's private return becomes a king's state procession, with the same city now seeing him as a husband and sovereign.

source_issues: 2503, 2506-2509, 2511-2517, 2522-2526: stanzas printed in eight half-lines and joined into four lines by the build.
2504, 2512, 2518-2520: lines garbled or corrupt in the edition's printing; readings marked uncertain.
2511: தத்தை addresses the parrots, but the edition's wording may mean the speaker is a woman named Tattai; read as parrots.
